extracted.intended_audience: health researchers, clinicians, and statisticians assessing interrater reliability in studies
extracted.subtask_description: Measuring and interpreting agreement between data collectors/raters in health research, contrasting percent agreement with Cohen's kappa, explaining calculation and limitations, and recommending acceptable thresholds for healthcare studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of interrater reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: The importance of rater reliability lies in the fact that it represents the extent to which the data collected in the study are correct representations of the variables measured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measurement of the extent to which data collectors (raters) assign the same score to the same variable is called interrater reliability; ensuring rater reliability supports validity of study data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Percent agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditionally interrater reliability was measured as percent agreement, calculated as the number of agreement scores divided by the total number of scores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple to compute but critiqued for inability to account for chance agreement (Cohen, 1960); should be interpreted with caution when chance agreement is likely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cohen's kappa
rubrics_metrics.description: Cohen's kappa was developed to account for the possibility that raters actually guess on at least some variables due to uncertainty; like most correlation statistics, the kappa can range from -1 to +1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frequently used to test interrater reliability because it adjusts for chance agreement; introduced as an improvement over percent agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations and interpretation of kappa
rubrics_metrics.description: While the kappa is one of the most commonly used statistics to test interrater reliability, it has limitations. Judgments about what level of kappa should be acceptable for health research are questioned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cohen's suggested interpretation may be too lenient for health-related studies because it implies that a score as low as 0.41 might be acceptable; users should be cautious and consider context-specific standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended minimum levels for kappa and percent agreement in healthcare
rubrics_metrics.description: Kappa and percent agreement are compared, and levels for both kappa and percent agreement that should be demanded in healthcare studies are suggested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article argues for demanding higher levels of agreement in healthcare research than some traditional interpretations recommend (exact numeric thresholds are provided in the full text rather than the abstract).

rubrics_metrics.name: Graphical representation and transformation (squared kappa)
rubrics_metrics.description: Graphical representation of amount of correct data by % agreement or squared kappa value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figure 2 demonstrates the relationship between percent agreement and (squared) kappa as ways to represent the amount of correct data; transformations like squaring kappa are used to map kappa to interpretable scales (details in full text/figures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Kappa calculation procedure and worked example
rubrics_metrics.description: Data for kappa calculation example and stepwise calculation of the kappa statistic are provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figures include contingency table/data and show the calculation steps (observed agreement, expected agreement, and kappa computation) to guide application in empirical studies.
